title: Kelvin waves can raise water levels along the US West Coast
summary:
Some ocean waves never curl over and crash onto a beach. Kelvin waves are broad bulges of water that move through the ocean and can raise the sea level along a coast.

In an AP report, experts forecast a series of these waves along the United States’ West Coast from October through February. They predict water levels could rise by six inches to a foot as the waves travel north along California toward Oregon and Washington.

These waves are not tsunamis. They are so broad that people cannot see them as an ordinary wave, and they do not make boats bob up and down, says scientist Dillon Amaya.

The process begins with winds near the equator, the imaginary line around Earth’s middle. Winds usually push Pacific water west toward Asia. When those winds weaken or reverse, a bulge of water can move east. After reaching South America, it travels along the coast to the north and south.

Kelvin waves are common during El Niño, a natural climate pattern involving warmer ocean water. Experts say the especially strong El Niño described in the report could increase their effects.

A higher sea level gives tides and storms a higher starting point. That can increase flooding and erosion, the wearing away of beaches. Some coastal communities already face these problems.

The waves also warm the ocean and push cold, nutrient-rich water deeper, affecting marine life. Their effects will depend partly on how they combine with tides, storms and other waves.
why_it_matters: Understanding Kelvin waves helps explain why tides and storms can bring more water onto beaches when the sea level is already higher.
